prompt.context: Our client is a for-profit, specialty college named Chic Cosmetology University (CCU). Founded in 2005, CCU is a program for high school graduates seeking their professional cosmetology license. CCU is currently the market leader for cosmetology education with campuses in ten major metropolitan areas in the US.
prompt.question: CCU has capital to invest in a new campus and is considering Chicagoland as a location – should they do it?

clarifying_info.q: What is CCU's goal for the new campus?
clarifying_info.a: Achieve positive operating profit for the new campus two years after opening.
Enrolled students take classes at a physical campus for one school year to earn their degree. The fiscal year begins on September 1.
CCU has the best campuses and equipment in the industry, and boasts strong job placement into top local salons.

clarifying_info.q: How fast is the industry growing?
clarifying_info.a: CCU and industry enrollments are growing at 5% per year.
There are 2-3 other large specialty colleges and lower-cost community colleges.

clarifying_info.q: What credentials are required to enter the cosmetology field?
clarifying_info.a: A high school diploma and a cosmetology degree are both required.

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost of building the Chicagoland campus?
clarifying_info.a: The initial Chicagoland campus costs $4.5M in initial building costs to renovate the chosen site. These costs can be amortized evenly over a three-year period. Assume fixed costs remain flat per year.

exhibits.title: CCU 2010 Financials (31-Aug-2010)
exhibits.shows: A financial summary table for all CCU campuses combined, showing enrollment count, revenue from enrollments, fixed campus costs (broken into buildings/equipment and recruiting/G&A), variable campus costs (broken into instructors and student supplies), and operating profit. All figures are in thousands of dollars.

exhibits.title: CCU and Major Competitor Locations (31-Aug-2010)
exhibits.shows: A table listing CCU's ten existing campus cities along with the 2010 market share (percentage of total potential students as defined by CCU) for each city, and a map legend distinguishing CCU campus locations from major competitor campus locations.

data.share_definition: Share of total potential students as defined by CCU

framework: 1. Revenue structure: Determine revenue per student and total revenue potential
2. Cost structure: Break down fixed and variable costs per campus; calculate annual fixed costs including amortization
3. Break-even analysis: Compute gross profit per student and number of enrollments needed to break even
4. Market sizing: Estimate the pool of potential CCU students in Chicagoland
5. Market share projection: Use competitive landscape data to project realistic enrollment
6. Recommendation: Compare projected enrollments to break-even; assess feasibility and alternatives

questions.prompt: How many students will CCU need to break even in Year 1?
questions.guidance: Candidate should derive per-campus financials from the aggregate Exhibit A data (10 campuses, 10,000 students), then layer in the amortized Chicagoland investment. Key steps: (1) average revenue per student = $15K, (2) variable cost per student = $8K, (3) gross profit per student = $7K, (4) annual fixed cost per campus = $4.8M, (5) amortization of $4.5M over 3 years = $1.5M/yr, (6) total annual fixed cost = $6.3M, (7) break-even enrollments = 900.

math.setup: Scale aggregate financials from 10 campuses down to 1 campus, then add annual amortization of the $4.5M investment.
steps: Revenue per student = $150,000K / 10,000 students = $15K per student
Variable cost per student = $80,000K / 10,000 students = $8K per student
Annual fixed cost per campus = $48,000K / 10 campuses = $4,800K = $4.8M
math.answer: CCU needs 900 enrolled students per year to break even in Year 1.

questions.prompt: What types of schools and students does CCU target in Chicagoland? (Brainstorm)
questions.guidance: See brainstorming section. After candidate identifies several criteria, reveal that CCU has identified 1,000 targeted high schools in the Chicagoland area, and CCU's market research estimates an average of 6 students per HS have 'potential' for CCU enrollment.

questions.prompt: What is the highest market share CCU Chicago could expect to capture in Year 1, and how many enrollments does that represent?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use Exhibit B to observe that campuses facing one competitor tend to have ~10% share, while those with no competitor have ~15%. Boston has 8% share with only one competitor, suggesting 10% is a reasonable upper bound. Total potential students = 1,000 HS x 6 students = 6,000 from HS market. Since 80% of enrollments come from HS and 20% from the adult market, total potential market = 6,000 / 0.80 = 7,500. At 10% market share, projected enrollments = 750. This is 150 short of the 900 break-even threshold.

math.setup: Determine total potential market using HS pipeline, then apply projected market share.
steps: HS potential students = 1,000 high schools x 6 students/HS = 6,000
HS students represent 80% of total enrollment pool, so total potential = 6,000 / 0.80 = 7,500
Projected market share = 10% (one competitor present; analogous to Houston and other single-competitor markets)
math.answer: CCU could capture approximately 750 students in Year 1, which is 150 below the 900 break-even threshold.

questions.guidance: Candidate should clearly state CCU should NOT enter the Chicago market under the current cost structure. Strong candidates will also surface several qualitative alternatives and mitigants. Outstanding candidates note that the 10% share benchmarks are for campuses operating at least 3 years, so Year 1 and Year 2 are likely even lower, making the case against entry even stronger.

brainstorming.prompt: What types of schools and students do you think CCU targets?

categories.name: Target Schools
ideas: Public high schools (private HS graduates more likely to pursue 4-year university)
High schools in middle-class areas (affordability concerns for low-income students)
High schools geographically close to the campus

categories.name: Target Students
ideas: Students not planning to attend a 4-year college
Students with an interest in cosmetology as a career

recommendation: CCU should NOT enter the Chicagoland market under the current cost structure. Projected Year 1 enrollment of ~750 students falls 150 short of the 900-student break-even threshold, and the 10% market share benchmark reflects mature campuses (3+ years old), meaning actual Year 1 share is likely even lower.
risks: Year 1 and Year 2 enrollment will likely underperform the 10% benchmark since that figure applies to established campuses, making break-even in two years highly unlikely
Fixed costs of $6.3M per year (including amortization) create significant downside if enrollment is below projections
Competitive pressure from existing large specialty colleges and lower-cost community colleges may further suppress market share
next_steps: Consider offering scholarships or financial incentives to increase the potential student pool and conversion rate
Evaluate other cities without a CCU presence where market share could be higher
Explore adding a second campus in a high-share market such as NYC where demand may exceed current capacity
Conduct further market research in candidate cities to validate potential per target high school
Identify ways to reduce fixed costs, such as transporting equipment and materials from campuses not at full capacity
Assess whether a smaller initial investment (e.g., $300K vs. $4.5M) could change the break-even math, though the low Year 1 share still makes profitability within two years unlikely
